edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SPORT + SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY
edition.deck: The stories shaping the day, from protests in France and a failed execution in Tennessee to a major Danish data breach.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential current affairs and substantive reporting across the three sections. Related coverage of the same event is grouped; unconfirmed claims and unsettled outcomes remain attributed.

content.headline: Christa Pike is conscious after surviving a failed execution, lawyers say
content.shortHeadline: Pike is conscious after failed execution attempt
content.standfirst: The Tennessee prisoner is speaking and receiving hospital care after surviving two doses of an execution drug, her lawyers say. Her prognosis remains unclear, and authorities have not said whether they will try again.

image.caption: Christa Pike in a courtroom in Knoxville, Tennessee, in December 2007.

sources.originalTitle: US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after botched execution attempt, lawyers say

segments.body: Christa Pike, 50, is conscious and speaking after surviving a failed lethal-injection attempt in Tennessee last week, her lawyers say. She remains in hospital receiving critical care, with severe arm injuries and an uncertain prognosis.

segments.title: Questions over what went wrong
segments.body: Pike’s defence team says she was given two doses of pentobarbital after officials struggled to establish intravenous access. Anaesthesiologist Joel Zivot, advising the defence, has said the drug may have spread into tissue rather than entering her bloodstream; the amount absorbed and the extent of any lasting harm remain unknown.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports witnesses heard Pike choking and struggling during the attempt, and quotes death-penalty abolitionist Helen Prejean describing the process as cruel. Her lawyers have asked Tennessee’s governor to commute her sentence.

content.headline: France school protests swell as police use tear gas and water cannon
content.shortHeadline: School protests spread across France amid clashes
content.standfirst: Hundreds of thousands joined demonstrations demanding better school conditions, while police used tear gas and water cannon in several cities. Injuries, arrests and allegations of excessive force are adding to pressure on the government.

image.caption: Riot police clash with school protesters in France as officers use tear gas.

sources.originalTitle: Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests grow across France
Riot police fire teargas as 250,000 take part in schools protests across France
How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?
‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing

segments.body: France’s government said more than 250,000 people demonstrated on Tuesday, while student unions put the total at 450,000. The protests, which began over overcrowded classrooms, staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, have spread from the Paris suburbs to cities across the country.

segments.title: Clashes and calls for change
segments.body: Police used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes. The government reported injuries among students, school staff and police; rights groups and unions have alleged disproportionate force. Authorities are investigating several incidents involving police weapons, while ministers say most police responses have been proportionate.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s explainer details complaints behind the demonstrations, including unequal educational opportunities, large classes, unreplaced absent teachers and buildings in need of repair. It also reports that France spends more than the OECD average on upper secondary education, while analysts question how the money is allocated.

content.headline: Russia’s plague-lab death remains unexplained as WHO seeks details
content.shortHeadline: WHO seeks answers after Russian lab worker’s death
content.standfirst: Russia says the 28-year-old researcher died of pneumonia of unknown cause, and that identified contacts have shown no symptoms. The WHO says there is no sign of a wider outbreak, but has urged Moscow to share timely information.

image.caption: The research institute where the worker was employed is in Irkutsk, Siberia.

sources.originalTitle: Rubio urges Russia to share more information on plague lab worker's death
Plague epidemic risk in Russia low after death of lab technician, WHO says
What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?
Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague. This is what you should know

segments.body: The cause of death of Darya Shipilova, a worker at a plague research institute in Siberia, has not been established. Russian authorities say tests have not confirmed plague and that contacts have been identified and are being monitored; none had shown symptoms in the information shared with the WHO.

segments.title: Uncertainty and public-health risk
segments.body: The WHO has reported no sign of a wider outbreak and assessed the risk as low for Russia overall and very low for Europe, according to its spokesperson. Experts say pneumonic plague can spread through close contact but is treatable with antibiotics if diagnosed early. It remains unconfirmed whether Shipilova had plague or how she became ill.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Russia to share complete and transparent information, citing conflicting accounts. It also reports that contacts were being monitored and that the WHO’s risk assessment varied by location.

content.headline: Nepal flood survivors face years-long wait for death certificates
content.shortHeadline: Nepal flood families face years-long wait for death certificates
content.standfirst: With thousands still missing after last month’s floods, relatives say they cannot access compensation or settle inheritance without death certificates. Nepal’s law generally requires a missing person to be presumed dead only after 12 years.

image.caption: A symbolic effigy made from sacred kusha grass allows families to perform last rites when a body cannot be recovered.

sources.originalTitle: Many Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo

segments.body: Families of people missing after the deadly floods on the China-Nepal border are struggling to have their relatives legally declared dead. The government has ended rescue operations, but more than 5,000 people remain missing, and relatives say officials have turned them away when they seek death certificates.

segments.title: Compensation and rebuilding
segments.body: Certificates are required to access funeral and bereavement payments and to deal with property and inheritance. Nepal’s civil law generally presumes a missing person dead only after 12 years, and does not specifically provide for a disaster on this scale. The government says it is considering a solution and may amend the law as families wait for support.

content.headline: Trump’s ‘take out’ remark about California cities draws sharp backlash
content.shortHeadline: Trump’s remark about California cities sparks backlash
content.standfirst: Donald Trump said Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego, prompting California leaders to condemn his words. The White House said he was warning that a nuclear-armed Iran could threaten US cities.

image.caption: Donald Trump speaks at a campaign rally in Nebraska.

sources.originalTitle: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego

segments.body: At a rally in Nebraska, President Donald Trump said Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego while discussing the conflict with Iran. California Governor Gavin Newsom called the remarks dangerous and said the state would monitor for any threat; the mayors of both cities also criticised his comments.

The White House said Trump meant that US cities would have been threatened if Iran had developed a nuclear weapon, and rejected what it called a media “freakout”. The account says the president has not responded to the California leaders’ statements. The reporting does not establish that the remarks reflected a specific threat to either city.

content.headline: Paramount completes $110bn Warner Bros merger under new safeguards
content.shortHeadline: Paramount completes $110bn Warner Bros merger
content.standfirst: The merger creates a major entertainment group and brings CNN and CBS under one corporate owner. A settlement requires film releases and establishes a news-independence board, while analysts warn that debt, job cuts and future price rises remain concerns.

image.caption: The Paramount-Warner Bros merger brings major film and television brands under one owner.

sources.originalTitle: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you

segments.body: Paramount Skydance has completed its $110bn takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, combining major film and television studios, streaming services and franchises. The company will operate as Skydance Corporation, with David Ellison as chairman and chief executive.

segments.title: Costs and conditions
segments.body: A settlement with US states requires the merged studio to release at least 30 films annually for the first two years and 32 in each of the next three, including independent films. It also establishes a board for editorial independence at CNN and CBS. Analysts expect the company’s substantial debt and planned cost savings to put pressure on workers and consumers.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s consumer-focused reporting says analysts expect streaming prices to rise over time as the company seeks profitability. A report cited by the BBC estimates the merger could eliminate about 4,500 direct film and television jobs, while the settlement does not prevent layoffs.

content.headline: Former Australian bishop jailed for abusing two young Aboriginal men
content.shortHeadline: Former Australian bishop jailed for sexual abuse
content.standfirst: Christopher Saunders, 76, was sentenced to six and a half years after being convicted of rape and 12 counts of indecent assault. He will be eligible for parole in February 2031.

image.caption: Former Bishop of Broome Christopher Saunders.

sources.originalTitle: Former Australian bishop jailed for sexually abusing young men

segments.body: Former Bishop of Broome Christopher Saunders has been jailed for sexually abusing two young Aboriginal men while serving as a Catholic cleric. A Western Australian court found him guilty of one count of rape and 12 counts of indecent assault.

The court heard that Saunders groomed the young men, inviting them to gatherings and supplying alcohol, sometimes using church funds and properties. One victim said in a statement that he struggled to speak about what happened. Saunders resigned as bishop after allegations first emerged in 2020.

content.headline: Human activity is changing how a Himalayan pheasant communicates
content.shortHeadline: Himalayan monal changes its calls amid human pressure
content.standfirst: Two Indian studies found that Himalayan monals in noisier places made higher-pitched, shorter calls, while habitat pressure is pushing the birds higher into the mountains. Researchers say the findings are preliminary and the wider ecological consequences need more study.

image.caption: A male Himalayan monal, whose plumage includes green, blue and copper feathers.

sources.originalTitle: A beautiful Himalayan bird is changing its voice due to human activity, research shows

segments.body: Researchers recorded more than 700 calls from Himalayan monals in two Uttarakhand valleys. Birds at the busier tourist site made calls with higher peak frequencies and shorter durations than those in the quieter valley, findings the researchers link to background noise.

segments.title: Habitat under pressure
segments.body: A separate study modelled how climate change could shrink and fragment suitable habitat for the species across parts of the Indian Himalayas through 2100. Researchers also say tourism and infrastructure are crowding the bird’s habitat. The studies are preliminary: the researchers caution that further work is needed to establish ecological consequences.

content.headline: Equinor warns UK could deter investment if North Sea fields are rejected
content.shortHeadline: Equinor warns UK oil decisions could deter investment
content.standfirst: The Norwegian state energy company says it will reconsider future UK investment if Rosebank and Jackdaw are not approved. Environmental campaigners dispute the case for new drilling, and the government says it will weigh all relevant evidence.

image.caption: Equinor chief executive Anders Opedal has warned the company may reassess future UK investment.

sources.originalTitle: UK risks being 'uninvestable' if new oil and gas fields not approved, warns Equinor

segments.body: Equinor chief executive Anders Opedal says the company would take a “hard view” of future UK investment if approval is refused for Rosebank and Jackdaw. The government is considering the projects after an earlier consent was delayed by a court ruling on climate impacts.

segments.title: Energy security and climate concerns
segments.body: Equinor argues that new North Sea production could support UK supply as domestic output is forecast to fall. Campaign group Uplift says Rosebank would produce oil mainly for export and would not cut household bills. The government says its decision will consider environmental assessments and public submissions.

content.headline: Seventh person arrested over incident near RAF Fairford; no one charged
content.shortHeadline: Seventh arrest made over RAF Fairford incident
content.standfirst: A 22-year-old British man was arrested in London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Police say the investigation remains live; no one has been charged, and reported claims of an Iranian drone plot have not been verified.

image.caption: RAF Fairford, the Gloucestershire airbase at the centre of the investigation.

sources.originalTitle: British national arrested in connection with RAF Fairford incident

segments.body: Counter-terrorism police have arrested a 22-year-old British national in connection with an incident near RAF Fairford on 27 September. It is the seventh arrest; the earlier six people were released on bail, and no charges have been announced.

segments.title: Unresolved security questions
segments.body: The investigation began after three vehicles were reported near the Gloucestershire airbase, prompting evacuations. US bombers have since left the base. President Donald Trump referred to threats, but the BBC says it has not verified media reports that Iran was plotting a drone attack.

content.headline: UK makes last effort to keep its East Jerusalem consulate open
content.shortHeadline: UK seeks to stop Israel closing East Jerusalem consulate
content.standfirst: The consulate handles British relations with Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza. Israel has threatened to close it in response to UK sanctions on settlements; a diplomatic stand-off could further damage relations.

image.caption: The British consulate in East Jerusalem handles relations with Palestinians in the city and the occupied territories.

sources.originalTitle: UK to make last-ditch effort to stop Israel closing East Jerusalem consulate

segments.body: The UK is trying to persuade Israel not to close its East Jerusalem consulate, a mission first established in 1838. Israel set a deadline of Thursday, linking the threatened closure to British sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The Foreign Office has not commented on reports that Britain could expel Israeli diplomats if the consulate shuts. Former ambassador Matthew Gould warned that such a move would seriously damage cooperation in defence, security and technology; a deal to keep the mission open has not been announced.

content.headline: Labour figures rule out cooperation with Greens after party’s Zionism vote
content.shortHeadline: Labour rejects future cooperation with Greens after vote
content.standfirst: Green members adopted a policy treating Zionism as racism and calling for a single Palestinian state. Labour figures say cooperation is now unlikely, while the Greens’ leader has said antisemitism and criticism of Israel must remain distinct.

image.caption: Green Party leader Zack Polanski at the party conference.

sources.originalTitle: Labour figures rule out working with Greens after ‘Zionism is racism’ vote

segments.body: Senior Labour figures say working with the Greens has become very unlikely after the party adopted a policy treating Zionism as a form of racism and calling for a single Palestinian state. The policy passed at the Green conference by 1,022 votes to 813, despite opposition from four of the party’s five MPs.

segments.title: Political consequences
segments.body: Labour chair Bridget Phillipson called the vote shameful, and some within Labour want the party to formally rule out future arrangements with the Greens. Zack Polanski stopped short of endorsing or criticising the motion, saying antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state “are and must always be completely distinct”.

content.headline: Gosport seeks help with costs after anti-migrant protest turns violent
content.shortHeadline: Gosport seeks funds after anti-migrant protest
content.standfirst: The council says three protests linked to planned small-boat arrivals have cost at least £350,000 to police, with further clean-up costs after disorder on Sunday. The Home Office says contingency plans are in place and praised police handling of the demonstration.

image.caption: Police officers at the Gosport protest, where 12 people were arrested.

sources.originalTitle: Gosport, the anti-migrant flashpoint pleading not to become a permanent problem

segments.body: Gosport Borough Council leader Zoe Huggins says she will ask the Home Office to cover clean-up costs after a protest near Fort Blockhouse. Bins were set on fire and items used as barricades, according to the council; police made 12 arrests, including on suspicion of assaulting officers.

segments.title: Dispute over the processing site
segments.body: The council says it had raised concerns about the site and asked for the government’s risk assessment, but had not received a response. The Home Office says it will work with local partners to maintain public safety and has contingency plans for arrivals further along the coast. The migrants brought ashore on Sunday were transferred to Kent for processing.

content.headline: Staff shortages threaten promised specialist support for pupils with SEND
content.shortHeadline: Staff shortages threaten specialist SEND support
content.standfirst: The government’s £1.8bn Experts at Hand scheme aims to bring specialist support into mainstream schools, but councils and organisations warn they may not be able to recruit enough professionals. Ministers say the programme is being phased in over three years.

image.caption: Schools minister Georgia Gould, who has promoted the Experts at Hand scheme.

sources.originalTitle: SEND pupils’ extra support at risk with schools unable to access specialist staff

segments.body: The Experts at Hand programme, launched with £1.8bn over three years, is intended to give mainstream schools better access to educational psychologists, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and specialist teachers. At least 36 councils have raised concerns about whether enough qualified staff are available.

segments.title: Capacity to deliver
segments.body: A specialist charity says it has not received firm plans from the councils it works with, and school leaders warn that shortages already make support difficult to access. The Department for Education says the scheme is not stalling: local areas are beginning delivery and will build their offers over time as they recruit and train staff.

content.headline: New nursery guidance would restrict staff phone use and child photos
content.shortHeadline: Nursery phone and photo rules planned after abuse case
content.standfirst: Proposed guidance would ban personal devices in childcare areas and limit staff to one photo per child per day. The plans follow abuse and cyber incidents; safeguarding advocates say secure handling of images and adequate staff training will also matter.

image.caption: The planned guidance would restrict nursery staff’s use of digital devices around children.

sources.originalTitle: Nursery staff to be banned from using phones after ‘chilling’ child abuse case

segments.body: The government is preparing guidance telling nursery staff, childminders and visitors not to use personal phones or devices in childcare areas. Staff would use a designated work device, with filters, and take no more than one photo of each child a day, according to sources familiar with the plans.

segments.title: Safeguarding and implementation
segments.body: The guidance is being developed after a nursery worker was jailed for abusing children and following a cyberattack targeting a nursery chain. It would also require parental permission for images and regular checks of work devices. A union representative says staff shortages and uneven training could make the safeguards harder to apply.

content.headline: Businesses warn Tory plan to reverse EU food deal could raise costs
content.shortHeadline: Businesses warn Tory EU food-deal reversal risks prices
content.standfirst: The Conservatives say they would reverse a proposed UK-EU food and drink agreement if elected, objecting to automatic alignment with Brussels rules. Industry voices disagree on the deal’s merits but warn that repeated rule changes risk uncertainty and extra costs.

image.caption: A market stall selling fruit and vegetables in Birmingham.

sources.originalTitle: Brexit U-turn on food would drive up prices, supermarkets warn Tories

segments.body: The Conservatives have pledged to reverse any food and drink deal Labour makes with the EU, arguing that the UK should not automatically follow rules it cannot shape. The government is seeking an agreement intended to reduce checks on cross-border trade, with a deal expected before the end of the year.

segments.title: Business divided on the effects
segments.body: The Food and Drink Federation backs closer alignment, saying trade with the UK’s largest export market has suffered since Brexit and businesses need stable rules. Fresh-produce representatives warn that alignment could complicate imports from outside the EU. Retailers say the proposed deal may have only a small effect on prices but that uncertainty itself risks disrupting supply.

perspectives.body: The reporting captures a split within industry: the Food and Drink Federation favours the proposed agreement to ease trade, while the Fresh Produce Consortium argues that closer EU alignment could harm trade with other markets.

content.headline: Danish data breach exposes 8.8 million CPR records; identity checks tightened
content.shortHeadline: CPR data breach exposes 8.8 million records
content.standfirst: Unauthorised access to Denmark’s civil registration system exposed information on living and deceased people, according to reporting. Pharmacies are tightening identity checks, while experts say a CPR number alone should no longer be treated as proof of identity.

image.caption: DXC Technology Denmark, the company that operates the CPR system, is based in Valby.

sources.originalTitle: Her er firmaet, der driver cpr-systemet – og havde en rigtig dårlig mandag
Apoteker skærper opmærksomheden ved medicinudlevering efter CPR-læk
Kan jeg stole på det, jeg får i min e-Boks? Her er de spørgsmål, danskerne vil have svar på efter cpr-lækket

segments.body: A reported breach exposed 8.8 million CPR numbers over ten days in September, including records of living and deceased people. DXC Technology Denmark, which operates the system and other public-sector IT services, has not publicly responded in the supplied reporting. Authorities are investigating the incident.

segments.title: What people are being told
segments.body: Pharmacies say customers may be asked for health-card identification or control questions, especially when collecting medicines with a risk of misuse or picking up prescriptions for someone else. Security guidance says organisations should verify identity using information beyond CPR details. e-Boks says the leak alone does not give outsiders access to send messages through its service.

perspectives.body: DR’s security expert says the core risk is that some organisations have treated a CPR number as proof of identity. The expert says the breach also raises questions about monitoring how authorised users and third parties use access to sensitive systems.

content.headline: Politicians demand action after allegations of exploitation of 15 migrant auto ḿ
content.shortHeadline: Politicians demand action over alleged migrant-worker abuse
content.standfirst: Fifteen foreign mechanics are alleged to have faced coercion, poor living conditions and withheld pay at a North Zealand car business. The company’s director is in custody on suspicion of exploiting workers; the allegations have not been adjudicated.

sources.originalTitle: Rystede politikere reagerer på sag om "moderne slavehandel": - Jeg bliver ærlig talt rigtig vred

segments.body: TV 2 Kosmopol reports allegations that a North Zealand car company exploited 15 mechanics from Asia between 2022 and 2025. One owner and director has been held in pre-trial detention on suspicion of exploiting workers and human trafficking. The mechanics say they were underpaid, worked excessive hours and lived in poor conditions.

segments.title: Calls for scrutiny
segments.body: Politicians from several parties have questioned how the alleged mistreatment continued and whether the fast-track recruitment scheme and oversight failed. The company’s owners have not responded to the reporting; one other owner said he knew nothing of the case and denied that anyone was guilty. The relevant agency had not responded by the report’s deadline.

content.headline: Danish study will test psilocybin with therapy for anorexia
content.shortHeadline: Danish trial tests psilocybin treatment for anorexia
content.standfirst: A research project in Region Zealand will enrol 62 adult women whose anorexia has not improved with earlier treatment. Researchers will test psilocybin alongside therapy; the approach is experimental and its effectiveness is not yet known.

image.caption: Senior researcher Oliver Hovmand is involved in the study of psilocybin with therapy for anorexia.

sources.originalTitle: Svampestof skal testes mod ‘den mest dødelige psykiatriske lidelse’
Puk blev straffet, når hun ikke spiste – nu håber hun på bedre behandling

segments.body: Researchers in Region Zealand are beginning a trial of psilocybin, the active substance in some psychedelic mushrooms, combined with therapy for anorexia. The study plans to recruit 62 women over 18 who have previously undergone treatment that did not help.

segments.title: An experimental approach
segments.body: Researchers hope the drug-assisted sessions may help participants question rigid rules around food and exercise, but the trial is intended to investigate whether the treatment works. A former patient interviewed by DR says she sees a need for alternatives after years of treatment; her experience does not establish the trial’s effectiveness.

perspectives.body: Former patient Puk Hoppe Søe describes being punished during earlier treatment when she did not eat and says she hopes new options may help people who remain ill. The article presents her account as personal experience, not evidence of the new treatment’s outcome.

content.headline: Government proposes 900m kroner for Danish public schools in 2027
content.shortHeadline: Government proposes 900m kroner for schools
content.standfirst: The proposed annual funding includes 200m kroner for 100 schools where pupils perform poorly in Danish and maths, 200m for small rural schools and 500m for a general school boost. The amounts still require budget negotiations.

image.caption: The proposed school funding follows a historically poor PISA result.

sources.originalTitle: Regeringen vil afsætte 200 millioner til indsats på 100 udvalgte skoler

segments.body: The government plans to allocate 900 million kroner to public schools in its proposed 2027 budget. Of that sum, 200 million would support 100 schools where pupils are struggling in Danish and maths, 200 million would go to small rural schools, and 500 million would provide a general uplift.

The proposal follows a historically poor PISA result, according to the report. The funds have not yet been assigned to specific measures and must be agreed in budget negotiations. Education Minister Magnus Heunicke says more teachers, including two-teacher classes, are among the government’s priorities; Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has pointed instead to working conditions rather than a pay rise.

content.headline: Motorway around Copenhagen to gain lanes and noise-reducing asphalt
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen ring road set for lane expansion
content.standfirst: The plan would widen most of the 17-kilometre Motorring 3 to four lanes in each direction, add noise-reducing asphalt and lower the speed limit from 110 to 90 km/h. Work is expected to start in 2027.

image.caption: Most of Motorring 3 is planned to expand from three to four lanes in each direction.

sources.originalTitle: En af Danmarks mest trafikerede motorveje skal nu udvides

segments.body: The parties behind Denmark’s infrastructure plan have agreed to expand most of Motorring 3 around Copenhagen from three to four lanes in each direction. The proposal also includes noise-reducing asphalt and a speed-limit reduction from 110 to 90 km/h.

segments.title: Noise and trade-offs
segments.body: The motorway carries more than 145,000 vehicles a day. The Danish Road Directorate estimates the new asphalt could reduce noise by three to four decibels for about 40% of nearby homes. A local mayor welcomed the noise measures but said he would have preferred not to use the emergency lane as an extra traffic lane.

content.headline: Hunters seek invasive coypu spotted on the Wadden Sea island of Rømø
content.shortHeadline: Hunters search Rømø for invasive coypu
content.standfirst: The large South American rodent has been spotted several times on Rømø. Conservation and dike officials warn that its burrowing could undermine protective earthworks, but hunters have not yet caught the animal.

image.caption: A hunter waits near an area on Rømø where the coypu has been spotted.

sources.originalTitle: På vadehavsø jagter de invasiv gnaver: 'Den er en stor trussel'

segments.body: Regulatory hunters are searching for a coypu on Rømø after it was first spotted in September. The species, introduced to Europe for fur farming, is established south of the Danish border. Seven coypu were recorded in Denmark this year, up from two last year, according to the figures cited by DR.

Officials say coypu dig burrows in banks and dikes, raising concern on an island protected from storms and water by large earthworks. The animal has not yet been caught, and the reporting describes the risk of damage rather than confirmed damage at the site.

content.headline: 14,000-year-old plant remains found at archaeological site near Aarhus
content.shortHeadline: Ancient plant remains uncovered near Aarhus
content.standfirst: Moesgaard Museum researchers have found preserved leaves, twigs and other plant remains in layers formed at the end of the last ice age. The unusually intact deposits may help reconstruct how the landscape and vegetation changed.

sources.originalTitle: Museumsinspektør jubler over 14.000 år gamle fund

segments.body: An excavation at Lisbjerg, outside Aarhus, has uncovered plant remains estimated to be about 14,000 years old. Researchers found the material in sediment layers preserved in a dead-ice hollow formed as ice melted at the end of the last ice age.

The upper layers also contain Iron Age refuse and animal bones, including a bone thought to be from a bison. Archaeologists say the unusually intact sequence of layers can help them study changes in vegetation and the landscape over time; further excavation is planned.

content.headline: MobilePay to adopt Vipps name as Nordic wallet unifies its branding
content.shortHeadline: MobilePay will be renamed Vipps in Denmark
content.standfirst: The app’s name is due to change on 12 January as Denmark, Finland, Sweden and Norway use a common brand. Vipps MobilePay says the service will otherwise remain unchanged; nearly 4.7 million people use it in Denmark.

image.caption: The MobilePay app’s icon changes first; its name is due to change in January.

sources.originalTitle: MobilePay skifter navn

segments.body: MobilePay will be renamed Vipps in Denmark on 12 January, bringing the app’s name and logo into line with the Nordic mobile wallet used in Denmark, Finland, Sweden and Norway. The company says users will not need to take any action and the app will work as before.

MobilePay joined with Norway’s Vipps in 2022 to create a shared service usable across the Nordic countries. The company says the Danish app handles more than half a billion transactions a year and has nearly 4.7 million users.

content.headline: England's Nations League window reveals depth around Kane's core
content.shortHeadline: England's attacking core takes shape as Kane reaches 125 caps
content.standfirst: England beat the Czech Republic 3-0 as Harry Kane marked his record-equalling 125th appearance with two goals. The wider international window also gave Thomas Tuchel fresh evidence about his options.

image.caption: Harry Kane marked his 125th England appearance with two goals against the Czech Republic.

sources.originalTitle: Midfield options and a fab front four - what we've learned about England

segments.body: Kane scored twice in England's 3-0 win over the Czech Republic, drawing level with Peter Shilton on 125 caps. The captain now has 91 international goals, and his performance capped a Nations League window that included a 7-0 win in Croatia.

segments.title: Competition for places
segments.body: Tuchel has reason to consider a settled attacking quartet of Kane, Anthony Gordon, Bukayo Saka and Jude Bellingham, with Morgan Rogers another option. Trent Alexander-Arnold impressed on his return, while Lewis Hall strengthened his case at left-back alongside Gordon.

Alex Scott's strong debut in the Croatia rout was cut short by a thigh injury that could keep him out for two months, a blow for both England and Bournemouth. Elliot Anderson and James Garner also feature among Tuchel's midfield options.

content.headline: Scotland's 2-1 loss to Slovenia leaves Pocognoli facing questions
content.shortHeadline: Scotland beaten by Slovenia as Robertson says they were outfought
content.standfirst: Scotland led at half-time at Hampden but conceded twice after the break in a damaging Nations League defeat. Andy Robertson and Sebastien Pocognoli both said the performance fell short.

sources.originalTitle: Honeymoon over as Pocognoli's Scotland suffer domestic disharmony
'Outfought' and 'not good enough' - Robertson on Scotland defeat

segments.body: Ryan Christie's first-half goal put Scotland ahead, but Slovenia turned the match around after the break to win 2-1. The defeat followed Scotland's victory in North Macedonia and left their bid for second place in Group B1 looking less secure.

segments.title: Questions over the system
segments.body: Captain Andy Robertson called Scotland's display "not good enough" and said they had been outfought. Slovenia repeatedly found space behind the high line and through midfield; Pocognoli said his side were not proactive or strong enough in the duels.

Former Scotland captain Willie Miller questioned whether Pocognoli would persist with his preferred back three after Slovenia exposed gaps in it. The coach said the team would learn from the defeat; Scotland's next Nations League games are away to Switzerland and at home to North Macedonia in November.

content.headline: Ronaldo says he should be punished after leaving Portugal camp
content.shortHeadline: Ronaldo apologises for leaving Portugal camp but wants to continue
content.standfirst: Cristiano Ronaldo says he accepts responsibility for walking out of Portugal's Nations League camp, but alleges coach Jorge Jesus broke their agreement over his playing time. He says he is not retiring.

image.caption: Cristiano Ronaldo, Portugal's captain and record scorer.

sources.originalTitle: Ronaldo wants Portugal 'punishment' but not retiring

segments.body: Ronaldo says Portugal's football federation should punish him for leaving the squad after he was an unused substitute against Norway and learned he would not start against Denmark. He apologised to his team-mates and supporters, saying he should not have left.

segments.title: A dispute over an agreement
segments.body: The forward says he had agreed with Jesus to miss both matches to manage his fitness, but that the coach later told him he would play for 30 minutes against Norway. Ronaldo also says Jesus reneged on an agreement about how to explain the episode publicly. Jesus had said there was no rift and that Ronaldo remained welcome in the team.

Ronaldo says he will remain available after his suspension period if he is fit and playing for his club. Portugal won both matches without him and next play their final Nations League group games against Denmark and Wales in November.

content.headline: Everton extend unbeaten run as Manchester City beat Sunderland 5-3
content.shortHeadline: Everton keep unbeaten run going; City win eight-goal thriller
content.standfirst: Everton continued their unbeaten run with a win over 10-man Ipswich, while Manchester City beat Sunderland 5-3. Brighton also ended champions Arsenal's perfect start, according to BBC Sport's Premier League round-up.

sources.originalTitle: Premier League

segments.body: Everton's unbeaten run continued with a victory over 10-man Ipswich. Manchester City beat Sunderland 5-3 in an eight-goal match to move three points clear at the top of the Premier League table.

Brighton beat Arsenal to end the champions' perfect start, while Leeds inflicted a heavy defeat on Newcastle to climb to third. The round-up also reports Leeds drawing with Crystal Palace and Coventry earning their first points of the season against Nottingham Forest.

content.headline: LIV Golf secures possible $300m financing as restructuring continues
content.shortHeadline: LIV Golf lines up possible $300m financing for 2027
content.standfirst: The proposed funding from BC Partners Credit is intended to help LIV Golf emerge from US bankruptcy protection and prepare for 2027. It remains subject to court approval, with the league's player line-up still uncertain.

sources.originalTitle: LIV Golf secures potential $300m investment

segments.body: LIV Golf has secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit as it tries to move forward with a 2027 season. The league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, and hopes to complete restructuring in early 2027.

segments.title: Players and funding remain unresolved
segments.body: The proposed financing is subject to bankruptcy court approval and other conditions. The amount LIV needs to start next season and which players will take part remain unclear. Players are owed at least $45m, and discussions over their terms have been extended to 25 October; they are not obliged to sign on to a new version of the league.

content.headline: Djokovic claims 102nd title after De Minaur retires from China Open final
content.shortHeadline: Djokovic wins 102nd title as De Minaur retires injured
content.standfirst: Novak Djokovic led Alex de Minaur by a set when the Australian retired with an apparent thigh injury in Beijing. Daniil Medvedev's semi-final disqualification was another major China Open talking point.

image.caption: Alex de Minaur retires injured during the China Open final against Novak Djokovic.

sources.originalTitle: 'Means more than just a trophy' - Djokovic claims 102nd title of career
Calm in real life but demons on court - Medvedev runs out of chances

segments.body: Djokovic was leading De Minaur 7-6 (7-3), 0-1 when the Australian retired after taking a medical timeout for an apparent left thigh problem. It was Djokovic's 102nd career title and extended his run of winning at least one singles title in every year since 2005.

segments.title: A turbulent Beijing semi-final
segments.body: Djokovic reached the final after beating Alexander Zverev and moving ahead of Daniil Medvedev, who was defaulted after hitting a ball into the stands and striking a spectator. Medvedev apologised and said he hoped to apologise to the spectator in person; he will lose the prize money and ranking points from his run to the semi-finals.

Medvedev's disqualification came after previous on-court outbursts, including a heavy fine for his conduct at the 2025 Australian Open. Djokovic said the Beijing trophy meant more than a single tournament, after a year in which physical and health problems had limited his schedule.

content.headline: Sinner ends 2026 season early because of ongoing knee injury
content.shortHeadline: Sinner rules himself out for rest of season with knee injury
content.standfirst: The world number one has not played since defending his Wimbledon title in July. He says he will prioritise treatment and his long-term career, leaving him unable to defend several end-of-year titles.

sources.originalTitle: Sinner out for rest of season with knee injury

segments.body: Jannik Sinner will not play again in 2026 because of an ongoing right knee injury. He said he and his doctors had decided he needed a course of treatment, adding that he would do everything possible to return at full fitness.

The Italian has been absent since defending his Wimbledon title in July. His early end to the season means he cannot defend points from titles in China, Vienna, Paris and the ATP Finals; BBC Sport reports that Alexander Zverev is all but guaranteed to replace him as world number one by year's end.

content.headline: Mandhana replaces Harmanpreet as India captain across all formats
content.shortHeadline: Mandhana takes over as India captain from Harmanpreet
content.standfirst: Harmanpreet Kaur has stepped down after leading India to a first global title in last year's 50-over World Cup. Smriti Mandhana, who has already captained the side in limited-overs cricket, takes over.

image.caption: Harmanpreet Kaur, who has stepped down as India's captain across all formats.

sources.originalTitle: Mandhana replaces Harmanpreet as India captain

segments.body: Harmanpreet Kaur has left the India captaincy across Tests, one-day internationals and T20s. She led the side to its first global title, the 50-over World Cup last year, and also captained India to a Test victory over England at Lord's in July.

Smriti Mandhana replaces Harmanpreet. She has previously captained India in 18 T20s and four ODIs, and led Royal Challengers Bengaluru to two Women's Premier League titles. India are due to host Zimbabwe for three T20s and three ODIs from 16 October.

content.headline: African music is more than Afrobeats: why the label can limit it
content.shortHeadline: African music is more than Afrobeats
content.standfirst: Artists and writers argue that using Afrobeats as a catch-all flattens a continent’s varied sounds. The label has helped music travel, but can obscure local scenes and leave emerging styles poorly documented.

image.caption: Tyla at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards in Los Angeles.

sources.originalTitle: The west has a blinkered view of African music – and it’s hurting the whole continent’s culture

segments.body: Tyla has objected to being grouped under Afrobeats, saying she represents South African amapiano. The Guardian traces how a label that helped market contemporary West African dance music came to stand in for a much broader range of African pop.

segments.title: What the label leaves out
segments.body: Artists including Tems and Burna Boy have also described their music in terms other than Afrobeats. The article argues that the umbrella can blur distinctions between traditions and leave newer styles—such as banku music, azonto and mara—without the documentation and local context needed to develop distinct identities.

content.headline: George Fenton, composer of scores for more than 100 films, dies aged 76
content.shortHeadline: Composer George Fenton dies aged 76
content.standfirst: The five-time Oscar nominee wrote music for Gandhi, Groundhog Day and many Ken Loach films, as well as landmark nature documentaries and BBC news programmes. His family said his death was unexpected; no cause was given.

image.caption: George Fenton in 2001.

sources.originalTitle: George Fenton, Oscar-nominated British composer for more than 100 films, dies aged 76

segments.body: George Fenton, the British composer whose work ranged across more than 100 feature films, television, theatre and documentary, has died aged 76. His family described his death as unexpected but did not give a cause.

segments.title: A career across screen and stage
segments.body: Fenton earned five Oscar nominations, beginning with Gandhi and Cry Freedom. His enduring collaborations included 18 Ken Loach films and repeated work with directors Stephen Frears and Richard Attenborough. He also composed for The Blue Planet, Planet Earth and Frozen Planet, and wrote themes for BBC news programmes including Newsnight.

content.headline: Liz Harris finds a restorative kind of togetherness with dream-pop trio Helen
content.shortHeadline: Liz Harris finds a new side of herself with Helen
content.standfirst: The Grouper musician reflects on collaboration, a viral track fraudulently uploaded by someone else, and the DIY instincts that keep her wary of the music industry. Reforming Helen, she says, has brought a welcome sense of community.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris has built Grouper around solitary, atmospheric songs. In Helen, the dream-pop trio she formed with Jed Bindeman and Scott Simmons, she finds a different register: “I get to relax more in Helen,” she says, describing its collaborative process as restorative during a period of medical difficulties.

segments.title: The costs of sudden attention
segments.body: When Grouper’s “Poison Tree” gained an unexpected audience on TikTok, Harris discovered that someone else had fraudulently registered and uploaded the song, earning around six figures. She and her label were able to recover what she was owed, but she says fake uploads and remixes leave independent artists spending energy policing streaming platforms.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album turns protest into a family affair
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello puts protest at the heart of his solo album
content.standfirst: On Everyone Gets What They Want, the Rage Against the Machine guitarist makes an explicit case for anti-racist and anti-fascist music. He also credits his late mother’s activism with shaping his belief that ordinary people can change the world.

image.caption: Tom Morello.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes Everyone Gets What They Want as his first full-length solo rock album with him at the microphone. He calls it a “State of the Union address”: a collection of anti-racist and anti-fascist songs, featuring guests including Serj Tankian and Kneecap, and his 15-year-old son Roman.

segments.title: The example of Mary Morello
segments.body: Morello says his mother, Mary, who died in June aged 102, taught him to act on behalf of others. He recalls her explaining the United Farm Workers grape boycott when he was six: “We have to help them because we can.” He has established a memorial project encouraging people to donate, volunteer and protest causes she supported.

content.headline: Tate Britain’s 90s exhibition revisits a decade of art, fashion and nightlife
content.shortHeadline: Inside the 90s: art, fashion and nightlife
content.standfirst: A selection of photographs and works from Tate Britain’s new exhibition evokes the decade’s overlapping scenes, from jungle at the Blue Note to club nights and fashion. Curator Edward Enninful says the period also changed who got to participate in culture.

sources.originalTitle: 'Rock 'n' roll swagger': 10 iconic images capturing the chaotic energy of '90s Brit culture

segments.body: The BBC looks at images featured in Tate Britain’s The 90s: Art & Fashion, including Corinne Day’s documentary-style photography, an Alexander McQueen runway show and Eddie Otchere’s portrait of Goldie’s Metalheadz night. Together they suggest a decade in which music, fashion, art and club culture repeatedly crossed paths.

segments.title: More than a style revival
segments.body: Curator Edward Enninful argues that the period was about more than its recognisable looks: he points to a wider shift in who could take part in culture and whose voices were heard. The article also revisits club photography, after-hours street scenes and the DIY energy that artists remember as distinctive to the time.

content.headline: Greg Freeman’s All Set the Bone turns small-town unease into restless rock
content.shortHeadline: Greg Freeman makes unease feel electric on All Set the Bone
content.standfirst: The Vermont songwriter’s new album pairs anxious, vividly detailed lyrics with compositions that veer through chord changes and sudden shifts. Pitchfork hears a darker, more menacing record than its predecessor.

sources.originalTitle: All Set the Bone

segments.body: Pitchfork describes Greg Freeman’s singing as deliberately unsteady: his voice cracks and slips across songs populated by angry, isolated people and struggling towns. The lyrics move quickly from sharply observed details to memorable turns of phrase, giving the album a nervous, unsettled point of view.

segments.title: Songs that threaten to come apart
segments.body: The music keeps pace with that instability. Built around guitars, piano and organ, the songs stretch beyond bar-rock convention through shifting tempos, chord changes and dynamic turns. With John Congleton producing, the record sounds darker than Freeman’s breakout Burnover, its heavier distortion adding to the sense of something barely held together.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul reissue reveals an album still in motion
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul remains a work in motion
content.standfirst: A deluxe edition gathers alternate mixes, outtakes and the US album alongside the original UK release. Pitchfork argues that the set makes the landmark record feel less like a fixed monument and more like a work shaped by choices and circumstance.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: Rubber Soul sits at a turning point in the Beatles’ history and in pop, as the band moved beyond songs as a string of hits toward an album conceived as a work in its own right. The new set’s recording notes also reveal how quickly the group worked under pressure to deliver a record by Christmas 1965.

segments.title: There is no single definitive version
segments.body: The collection includes the UK and US tracklists, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a new mix. Their differences invite comparisons without settling on one “real” Rubber Soul: the review finds pleasure in hearing how arrangements took shape, while noting that listeners’ preferences depend partly on which version they grew up with.

content.headline: Lambchop strip back their sound on the strange, intimate Punching the Clown
content.shortHeadline: Lambchop find new intimacy on Punching the Clown
content.standfirst: Kurt Wagner’s storytelling stays expansive as the band pares back its arrangements to acoustic guitar, banjo and choir. Pitchfork finds the result both disquieting and emotionally direct, with room for Wagner’s humour and tangents.

sources.originalTitle: Punching the Clown

segments.body: Lambchop have moved through many musical forms over four decades, but Kurt Wagner’s uncontainable writing remains a constant. On Punching the Clown, acoustic guitar, banjo and choral harmonies leave space for his generation-spanning stories, abrupt jokes and oddly precise observations.

segments.title: Plain arrangements, difficult feelings
segments.body: The stripped-back sound gives songs about illness, death and unfinished business an intimate, uneasy quality. The review hears a contrast between Wagner’s humour and the bleakness of the material, and argues that the album’s restraint helps it feel more emotionally direct rather than less ambitious.

content.headline: Artificial turns Sam Altman and OpenAI into a blunt, muddled satire
content.shortHeadline: Artificial’s OpenAI satire is sharp but muddled
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s film casts Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman in a comic account of OpenAI’s rise. The Guardian finds flashes of savage humour and chilling ideas, but says the film’s broad jokes and visual metaphors weaken its argument.

image.caption: Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.

sources.originalTitle: Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire

segments.body: Artificial follows Ilya Sutskever’s work with Geoff Hinton and his partnership with Sam Altman as OpenAI develops. Andrew Garfield gives Altman a calculated, self-pitying edge, while the film frames the company’s ambitions as a clash between Sutskever’s optimism and Altman’s self-interest.

segments.title: A satire that overstates its case
segments.body: The review sees moments of sharp comedy and genuine unease, but argues that the script’s broad humour and heavy-handed imagery leave little room to understand the people or the culture that enabled them. Its verdict: Artificial can point to dystopian risks, but its tonal jumble makes those warnings less persuasive.

content.headline: Twelve films to look out for at the 2026 London film festival
content.shortHeadline: Twelve films to look out for at the London film festival
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s selection ranges from Andrew Scott as actor Ian Charleson to a new Mike Leigh drama, a vampire in Vienna and a film about a Manchester teenager discovering its music scene.

sources.originalTitle: Hamlet’s goodbye, the last of Leigh, Birmingham blues and a vampire in Vienna: 12 great films at the London film festival

segments.body: The selection spans historical drama, contemporary social realism, comedy, science fiction and horror. Among the films highlighted are a portrait of Ian Charleson starring Andrew Scott, Carol Morley’s story of a teenager drawn into Manchester’s music scene, and Clio Barnard’s drama about young adults in Birmingham.

segments.title: A varied festival slate
segments.body: Other recommendations include a new film from Mike Leigh, an Andrew Haigh adaptation of a story by Colm Tóibín, and Isabelle Huppert as a vampire in present-day Vienna. The guide presents these as notable choices from the festival, rather than a claim that they share a single style or subject.

content.headline: Sergiu Celibidache’s son remembers the conductor behind The Yellow Tie
content.shortHeadline: A son remembers conductor Sergiu Celibidache
content.standfirst: In a personal essay tied to a new film he co-wrote, Serge Ioan Celebidachi recalls a loving but demanding father who rejected commercial recordings. He also explains why he secretly preserved recordings of his father’s performances.

image.caption: Sergiu Celibidache conducting in the early 1980s.

sources.originalTitle: Celibidache was a musical visionary, an uncompromising perfectionist – and my father

segments.body: Serge Ioan Celebidachi remembers his father, the conductor Sergiu Celibidache, as both generous and exacting. The musician expected full attention in everyday life as well as in music, and his son describes the pressure of those standards alongside the warmth of their relationship.

segments.title: The recordings he kept
segments.body: Celibidache believed that recordings could not reproduce the experience of live music and refused lucrative offers to make them. His son secretly allowed some orchestras to record later performances, believing those documents had value. That disagreement, he says, helped give him the distance to approach his father’s life without putting him on a pedestal.

content.headline: The Lost Children of Tuam is a devastating account of Ireland’s tragedy
content.shortHeadline: The Lost Children of Tuam refuses easy closure
content.standfirst: Monica Dolan plays historian Catherine Corless, whose research uncovered the fate of children at a mother and baby home in County Galway. The review praises the film’s restraint and its refusal to offer comforting resolution.

image.caption: Monica Dolan as historian Catherine Corless in The Lost Children of Tuam.

sources.originalTitle: The Lost Children of Tuam review – deeply serious retelling of Ireland’s devastating tragedy

segments.body: The film follows Catherine Corless as she investigates deaths at St Mary’s mother and baby home in Tuam. She finds nearly 800 death certificates but no burial records. The Guardian describes the drama as careful not to embellish or fictionalise the discoveries at the heart of the story.

segments.title: No simple ending
segments.body: Monica Dolan’s performance as Corless anchors the film, while brief appearances by survivors leave a lasting impression. The review stresses that the story offers neither a satisfying sense of closure nor an uplifting finish: its force lies in taking the people affected and the scale of the harm seriously.

content.headline: Club Kid is a warm, funny love letter to queer nightlife
content.shortHeadline: Club Kid finds heart in queer nightlife
content.standfirst: Jordan Firstman’s directorial debut follows a New York club promoter who discovers he has a 10-year-old son. The review praises its comic energy and its affection for nightlife without glossing over its messier realities.

image.caption: Miss Benny and Jordan Firstman in Club Kid.

sources.originalTitle: Club Kid review – Jordan Firstman’s heartfelt comedy is irresistible

segments.body: Peter, a Brooklyn club promoter played by Firstman, is forced to rethink his life when a former party acquaintance brings him the son he did not know he had. Their developing relationship gives the film its emotional centre, alongside a lively portrait of New York’s queer club scene.

segments.title: More than a redemption story
segments.body: The review resists reading the film as a simple warning against partying or an argument that parenthood fixes everything. Instead, it finds warmth in a story that acknowledges nightlife’s problems while showing why music, chosen family and shared spaces can matter. Firstman’s humour and the cast’s natural performances are singled out as strengths.

content.headline: James Dean was more than a rebel: the vulnerable actor behind the icon
content.shortHeadline: James Dean beyond the rebel image
content.standfirst: A new adaptation of East of Eden renews attention on Dean, whose career ended at 24. This account looks beyond the familiar image of youthful rebellion to the anxious, emotionally exposed performance that made him endure.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: The article revisits the making of Elia Kazan’s East of Eden, where Dean’s unpredictability unsettled co-star Raymond Massey but helped produce a performance of raw intensity. The film’s most affecting moments, it argues, show a desperate young man rather than the polished rebel of later iconography.

segments.title: A brief career, a lasting image
segments.body: Dean died in a car crash at 24, after only three starring roles. East of Eden was the only one he lived to see released. The account considers how his vulnerable screen presence, including the complicated longing in his performances, became inseparable from a posthumous legend that can overshadow the actor’s work.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility still speaks to the push and pull between heart and head
content.shortHeadline: Sense and Sensibility speaks to the heart-head struggle
content.standfirst: A new adaptation of Jane Austen’s first novel prompts a case for its relevance to a generation balancing emotional openness with caution and insecurity. The film itself, the review says, is darker and less consistent than the celebrated 1995 version.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Georgia Oakley’s adaptation.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility

segments.body: Austen’s sisters Elinor and Marianne respond differently to love and uncertainty: one restrains her feelings, the other invests heavily in romantic hope. The review connects their competing instincts to contemporary pressures around privacy, self-fulfilment and the difficulty of planning for an uncertain future.

segments.title: A new, uneven adaptation
segments.body: Georgia Oakley’s film is described as gloomier than the 1995 adaptation, with Daisy Edgar-Jones praised for conveying Elinor’s contained grief. The review finds the film uneven, but argues that Austen’s story still offers a useful way to think about the risks of suppressing feeling or mistaking romantic optimism for good judgement.

content.headline: Comédie Française turns opening-night chaos into a nimble farce
content.shortHeadline: Comédie Française makes backstage chaos funny
content.standfirst: This French comedy follows a theatre director through the three hours before Macbeth opens, as missing actors, backstage mishaps and a family complication threaten the performance. The review praises the cast’s precision and timing.

image.caption: A scene from Comédie Française.

sources.originalTitle: Comédie Française review – pre-show bedlam plays theatrical chaos for laughs

segments.body: Director Nina arrives without her staff pass and faces a mounting series of crises: a missing Lady Macbeth, unruly performers, technical problems and a visit from the culture minister. The comedy unfolds inside the Paris theatre as opening night approaches.

The review finds the film’s subplot about Nina’s former partner leaving their toddler with her less convincing than its backstage farce. Its strongest appeal is the ensemble’s comic timing and the affectionate picture it draws of theatre people determined to make the show go on.

content.headline: Damilola: The Untold Story remembers a child beyond the crime
content.shortHeadline: Damilola: The Untold Story centres the child and his friends
content.standfirst: John Boyega, his sister and others who knew Damilola Taylor recall the night he was killed and the grief that followed. The documentary focuses on their memories of a friend, rather than turning the case into conventional true crime.

image.caption: Damilola Taylor.

sources.originalTitle: Damilola: The Untold Story review – John Boyega’s trauma after losing his childhood friend is haunting

segments.body: The documentary brings together people who were among the last to see Damilola Taylor alive, including John Boyega, who remembers being frightened by the death of a child. His sister Grace recalls defending Damilola at school and later blaming herself for not walking him home.

segments.title: A community, not a crime scene
segments.body: The film also gives space to memories of North Peckham as a community, rather than reducing the estate to a stereotype. Its stylised recreations and indistinct archival footage avoid forensic spectacle. The review notes that the documentary does not investigate the Preddie brothers’ backgrounds, but says its focus remains with Damilola and those who have carried the loss.

content.headline: Pierre brings a new perspective to British police drama
content.shortHeadline: Pierre brings a fresh perspective to the British cop drama
content.standfirst: David Harewood plays a duty solicitor navigating police cases and institutional racism in a confident Channel 4 noir. The review sees the series as a notable step for Black British crime drama, despite occasional heavy-handed dialogue.

image.caption: David Harewood in Pierre.

sources.originalTitle: Pierre review – David Harewood’s twisty noir is an instant crime classic

segments.body: Pierre is a duty solicitor, not a police officer. When a young Black man who had been building a case of police harassment is found dead, the series draws its crime plot through Pierre’s work and his ties to the community. David Harewood’s performance gives the drama much of its authority.

segments.title: A wider remit than the usual cop show
segments.body: The review argues that Pierre’s position lets the series examine the everyday compromises and indignities of working around the police as a Black professional, while remaining rooted in his community. It praises the confident genre storytelling, though it finds some attempts to compress race and policing debates into dialogue too blunt.

content.headline: The Reluctant Vampire turns Eric Morecambe’s children’s books into comic fun
content.shortHeadline: The Reluctant Vampire is a family comedy with bite
content.standfirst: Lenny Rush leads an ensemble in this gag-filled adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s children’s books. The Guardian praises its warmth, surreal jokes and appeal to adults as well as children.

image.caption: Lenny Rush as Valentine in The Reluctant Vampire.

sources.originalTitle: The Reluctant Vampire review – Lenny Rush’s absolute joy of a comedy is perfectly cast

segments.body: Valentine is the disappointing second son in a vampire family: he has no fangs, dislikes blood and cannot fly. His mother eventually tells him he is human, rescued as a baby and raised as her own. The discovery sets off a string of misunderstandings and a gently developing friendship.

segments.title: A shared comic sensibility
segments.body: The review praises Lenny Rush and a supporting cast that includes Tom Davis, Sian Clifford, Bill Bailey and Ross Noble. It finds the series faithful to the books’ warmth and daftness while adding jokes for adults, and recommends giving it more than one episode to reach a particularly affectionate Morecambe-inspired gag.

content.headline: Lenny Rush on finding belonging in The Reluctant Vampire
content.shortHeadline: Lenny Rush on belonging and The Reluctant Vampire
content.standfirst: The 17-year-old actor discusses leading a comedy written for him, his admiration for David Brent and the messages he receives from families of disabled children. He sees Valentine’s awkwardness as a familiar story of trying to fit in.

image.caption: Lenny Rush as Val in The Reluctant Vampire.

sources.originalTitle: Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy

segments.body: Rush says the scripts for The Reluctant Vampire were written with him in mind. He describes the series as a family show that can genuinely work for everyone, and sees its young protagonist’s struggle to belong as relatable beyond the story’s vampires and gargoyles.

segments.title: Visibility and the work
segments.body: Rush says messages from parents whose disabled children have gained confidence from seeing him on screen made him realise the impact of his visibility. He also talks about his ambition to avoid being limited to comedy, his love of The Office, and the importance of his family keeping school and friendships in view alongside acting.

content.headline: Amy Dowden’s early Strictly exit raises questions about the show’s pairings
content.shortHeadline: Amy Dowden’s Strictly exit raises questions about pairings
content.standfirst: The professional dancer has left in the first week for a second consecutive year. The review argues that the show’s pairings shape its emotional appeal and that Dowden deserved a partner with a better chance to show her skill as a teacher and performer.

image.caption: Amy Dowden on Strictly Come Dancing.

sources.originalTitle: Amy Dowden’s exit exposes one big Strictly problem

segments.body: The piece argues that Strictly’s professional dancers, not just its celebrity contestants, are central to the show’s appeal. Their partnerships give viewers a reason to invest, as they help celebrities learn, take risks and change over the series.

segments.title: A difficult run
segments.body: Amy Dowden was paired with celebrity hairdresser Chris Appleton, who left in week one. The writer sets that early exit against Dowden’s recent years on the show, including injury and cancer treatment, and argues that her next series should be defined by her work with a partner rather than by her illness and resilience.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after its Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+, has no current Doctor and has cancelled a planned Christmas special. Fans and writers disagree about why the recent run faltered, while holding to the possibility of a return.

image.caption: The Doctors portrayed by Peter Capaldi, Christopher Eccleston, Matt Smith, David Tennant, Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: After the 2025 series starring Ncuti Gatwa, the BBC ended its partnership with Disney+ and put future production out to tender. No company has yet stepped forward, and the BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special. The show currently has no Doctor in place.

segments.title: A changing show, a loyal audience
segments.body: The article traces the series from its 1963 debut through its successful 2005 revival and the more recent change in Doctors and showrunners. Contributors differ over the causes of the latest decline, pointing to scripts, the pace of production and the Disney partnership; fans interviewed remain hopeful that the programme will return.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors makes a spectacular start with Richard E Grant
content.shortHeadline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors slip-up sets the series alight
content.standfirst: Grant accidentally tells Joe Lycett he is a Traitor moments after being chosen, turning a casting reveal into an instant cliffhanger. The review argues that the blunder only heightens the show’s unpredictable appeal.

image.caption: Richard E Grant in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Richard E Grant has already ruined The Celebrity Traitors. It’s brilliant

segments.body: After being selected alongside Maya Jama as a Traitor, Richard E Grant responds to Joe Lycett’s question by saying, “Oh, I’m a Traitor.” The review confirms it was a genuine mistake, and follows the cast’s confusion as Grant laughs about the slip while Jama considers how they might recover.

segments.title: Why the format still surprises
segments.body: The opening also sets up Ross Kemp’s early suspicions and a cliffhanger in which James Acaster and Amol Rajan must plead for a chance to be recruited. The writer credits the show’s celebrity cast and unpredictable behaviour with renewing the pleasures of a familiar reality-game format.

content.headline: The final 70 Up asks what its participants think of the experiment
content.shortHeadline: 70 Up ends by questioning its own legacy
content.standfirst: As the long-running documentary series concludes, its participants revisit not only their lives but the way they were represented. The final episodes include criticism of director Michael Apted and the limitations of reducing decades of experience to a few hours of television.

image.caption: Participants in the 7 Up documentary series as children.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A little pill of poison’: Why the cast of 70 Up came to resent it

segments.body: 70 Up brings the series that began in 1964 as Seven Up! to a close. The programme follows the surviving participants and reflects on lives shaped by circumstance, opportunity and change. Producer Helen Houston says the series has reached a natural endpoint.

segments.title: The people behind the portrait
segments.body: The finale also returns to participants’ dissatisfaction with how they were portrayed. Peter Davies describes leaving after a tabloid backlash; John Brisby says he disliked being cast as a token toff, and earlier footage shows Jackie Basset challenging Apted’s treatment of women. The series remains compelling, the review argues, but its subjects know that the edit can never contain a whole life.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has excellent combat but little else to sustain it
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day’s combat can’t save its repetition
content.standfirst: The prequel recreates the alien invasion that shaped the series, and its cover-based shooting feels better than ever. But the review finds repetitive levels, intrusive collectibles and too few ideas beyond the firefights.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day places Marcus Fenix and his squad at the start of the Locust invasion. The opening delivers the series’ familiar mix of destruction, tactical cover and chainsaw combat, and the review calls the movement and firefights the best the games have offered.

segments.title: A strong core stretched thin
segments.body: The praise is undercut by levels that repeatedly send players across the same spaces, large areas crowded with collectibles and side objectives, and moments when exploration can trigger a mission failure. The reviewer finds that the game’s strongest ideas arrive early, leaving its excellent combat surrounded by repetition.

content.headline: Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil recreates the feeling of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil captures the unease of playing the game
content.standfirst: The adaptation leaves familiar heroes aside to follow an ordinary courier through escalating danger, scarce ammunition and recognisable locations. The argument is that its fidelity lies in recreating the games’ structure and vulnerability, not simply their characters.

image.caption: Zach Cregger and Austin Abrams on the set of the Resident Evil film.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: The film follows courier Bryan Hodukavich as a virus outbreak engulfs Raccoon City. He starts without weapons or a clear understanding of events, then finds equipment while moving through an abandoned farmhouse, tunnel, hospital and sewer. Typewriters and fragments of recorded information echo the games’ conventions.

segments.title: A film shaped like a game
segments.body: The writer argues that Cregger’s approach reproduces the player’s uncertain progress through an unfamiliar world, rather than following familiar characters such as Leon or Claire. Its vulnerable protagonist recalls the series creator’s view that horror is strongest when survival never feels assured.

content.headline: How to protect children from Roblox phishing scams
content.shortHeadline: Roblox phishing scams target children’s accounts and Robux
content.standfirst: Fraudsters lure players to convincing fake login pages with promises of free in-game currency. Security experts advise opening Roblox directly and treating authentication codes like passwords.

image.caption: Roblox users are advised to use the official app or website and avoid unknown links.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children

segments.body: Scammers promise free Robux through links shared in YouTube or TikTok comments and Discord chats. The links lead to lookalike Roblox sign-in pages that collect usernames, passwords and sometimes two-factor codes before redirecting the child to the real site.

segments.title: Steps to reduce the risk
segments.body: NordVPN researchers say they found almost 200 addresses offering ready-made phishing pages during a seven-day period. The practical advice is to open Roblox through its official app or website rather than links, and never share authentication or backup codes. Roblox says it cannot guarantee it will restore lost currency or items.

content.headline: A father and son revisit the Call of Duty missions they first played together
content.shortHeadline: Replaying Call of Duty brings a father and son together
content.standfirst: Nearly two decades after playing Modern Warfare 2 together when his son was five, the writer returns to its co-op missions with him as an adult. The game becomes a way to rediscover teamwork, shared memories and time together.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game revisited by a father and son.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The pair return to missions they never completed the first time around. Their approaches still differ: the father advances cautiously, while his son charges ahead. They eventually learn to compromise, taking out the game’s notorious guard dogs first and completing a mission that has eluded them for 17 years.

segments.title: Play as a shared memory
segments.body: As they move through more missions, the writer reflects on the rare pleasure of playing without the pressure to make time productive. Their time in the flat is temporary, with the pair soon moving to different parts of the world, but his son tells him he will remember it as some of their best times together.

content.headline: The volunteer Pokémon professors who keep competitive play running
content.shortHeadline: Meet the volunteers behind Pokémon’s competitive tournaments
content.standfirst: At the 2026 world championships, volunteer professors served as judges, teachers and event staff. Their work ranges from checking results and explaining rules to helping players feel welcome and keeping the venue safe.

image.caption: Attendees at the 2026 Pokémon World Championships in San Francisco.

sources.originalTitle: Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling

segments.body: The Pokémon Professor Program is a global network of volunteers who help run official events. Around 300 professors attended the 2026 world championships in San Francisco, taking on roles that included refereeing card games, supporting players and managing event logistics.

segments.title: Rules, care and difficult calls
segments.body: Head judge Gemma Byard describes the work of checking match results, maintaining safety and handling disputes.
